item.title: A.I. Could Possibly End Humanity. How Are Humans Supposed to Process That?
item.description: The technology is far from the only existential risk our species faces. But weighing such cosmic fears can become a mind-bending exercise.
item.dc:creator: William J. Broad and Cade Metz

item.title: How the New iPhone Duo’s Glass Screen Bends Without Breaking
item.description: The screens of foldable phones are a triumph of materials science and microengineering.
item.dc:creator: William J. Broad
item.media:credit: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg, via Getty Images

item.title: The Mathematician Crushed Between OpenAI and Anthropic Over a Math Problem
item.description: Tristan Buckmaster was on the path toward an important proof when one of the A.I. giants used its staggering resources to get there first.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:credit: Graham Dickie for The New York Times

item.title: Could Your Chatbot Be Stealing Ideas From You? It’s a Thorny Question.
item.description: A controversy around OpenAI’s latest math proof raises a fear that might become increasingly common: that A.I. tools could take valuable insights from one user and hand them to another.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Kaoly Gutierrez for The New York Times
item.media:description: If someone types information into a chatbot, those details could turn up — days, months or years later — in a future iteration of that model.

item.title: Scientists Discover the Earliest Evidence of Drug Use in Really Old Teeth
item.description: A hunter-gatherer who lived in Indonesia as early as 25,000 years ago may have regularly sucked on betel nuts to release their psychoactive properties.
item.dc:creator: Becky Ferreira

item.title: Scientists Who Study Sleep and Narcolepsy Win Prestigious Lasker Award
item.description: Two researchers who study the debilitating sleep disorder have won a prestigious Lasker Award. Their research in animals laid the groundwork for a new drug that addresses the condition’s root cause.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson

item.title: OpenAI Says It Has Cracked One of Math’s ‘Millennium Problems’
item.description: The company’s announcement is the most dramatic sign yet that artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming the field of higher mathematics.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:description: Related to a set of equations about fluid mechanics, the “Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem” has long ranked among the great unsolved problems in mathematics.

item.title: What Is Navier-Stokes, the ‘Millennium’ Math Problem OpenAI Claims to Have Solved?
item.description: OpenAI announced today that it had solved the problem, one of seven “Millennium Problems” seen as among the most important in higher mathematics.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz

item.title: Top Mathematician Announces New Institute for A.I. Safety
item.description: Jacob Tsimerman, a recent recipient of the Fields Medal, believes that higher mathematics can help curb the dangers of runaway artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Siobhan Roberts
item.media:description: Canadian mathematician Jacob Tsimerman, who has announced the founding of the Mathematical A.I. Safety Institute (MAISI).

item.title: Racing to Contain Invasive Green Crabs in Puget Sound
item.description: Tribes and scientists are mounting an urgent trapping effort to keep European green crabs from devastating a corner of Puget Sound.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Dzombak and Chona Kasinger
item.media:credit: Chona Kasinger for The New York Times

item.title: Choking Global Trade
item.description: Low rainfall and shrinking rivers are causing shipping bottlenecks, and higher prices, around the world.
item.dc:creator: Claire Brown
item.media:description: The Rhine River near Düsseldorf, Germany, last month.

item.title: The Iran War Is Pushing Global Coal Use to Record Highs
item.description: Five years after virtually every world leader agreed to “phase down” the burning of coal for climate reasons, the fuel is more widely used than ever.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
Far East, South and Southeast Asia and Pacific Areas
item.media:description: Coal barges in East Kalimantan, Indonesia, last month.

item.title: August Ties for Hottest Month on Record
item.description: Sweltering summer temperatures put last month on par with July 2023 for global warmth, scientists said. More records could be broken in the months ahead.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong
item.category: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
item.media:description: A vendor cooled off with a frozen water bottle in a market in Seoul on Aug. 6.

item.title: States File 2 Lawsuits Over Trump’s Cuts to Endangered Species Act
item.description: Two lawsuits seek to reverse the Trump administration’s moves to open the habitats of imperiled wildlife to commercial activities.
item.dc:creator: Maxine Joselow
item.media:description: A San Joaquin kit fox, an endangered species native to central California. The fox, the smallest fox species in North America, is estimated to have 3,000 to 5,000 individuals remaining.

item.title: Toxic PFAS Cleanups at Military Sites Face Decades of Delay
item.description: The Pentagon has again postponed PFAS cleanups at hundreds of military sites, in some cases up to 19 years, prompting bipartisan anger in Congress.
item.dc:creator: Hiroko Tabuchi
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
Stewart Air National Guard Base (Newburgh, NY)
item.media:description: An email from the Pentagon to members of Congress said PFAS cleanups at nearly 243 military sites had been delayed.

item.title: A New Drug Lifts the Fog of Sleepiness for Those With Narcolepsy
item.description: The first-of-its-kind drug offers a reprieve for people who live with the debilitating sleep disorder.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson
item.media:credit: BSIP/Universal Images Group, via Getty Images
item.media:description: Patients with type 1 narcolepsy experience constant sleepiness and episodes of cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle control often triggered by happy emotions.

item.title: California’s Ambitious Plan for Textile Waste
item.description: A recycling law coming into force now could change fashion.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Cernansky
item.media:description: A recycling center in Stockholm. California is trying to build a network for textile waste from scratch.

item.title: U.S. to Lend $1.9 Billion to Restart a Shuttered Nuclear Plant in Iowa
item.description: No company in the United States has ever restarted a reactor that was seemingly closed for good, but there are now three major efforts underway to do so.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.media:credit: Nick Rohlman/The Gazette, via Associated Press
item.media:description: The Duane Arnold Energy Center near Palo, Iowa, in January 2025.

item.title: A Newer Kind of Gene Editing Promises to Edit ‘Nurture’ Over ‘Nature’
item.description: Traditional gene editing rewrites DNA. But a new approach, called epigenome editing, aims to treat the molecular scars we collect throughout our lives.
item.dc:creator: Emily Baumgaertner Nunn

item.title: Early Data Indicates an A.I.-Generated Drug Could Slow Aging
item.description: Artificial intelligence was used to help develop a drug candidate, rentosertib, for a rare lung condition. Its maker says the drug also seems to reduce the biological hallmarks of age.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:description: Rentosertib, Insilico Medicine’s small-molecule drug candidate developed and designed using generative A.I. for treating chronic lung disease, at the company’s research and development facility in Shanghai.

item.title: How Ancient Farmers Used Floral Designs to Track Goods
item.description: A Mesopotamian culture’s decorated ceramics show some early roots of math, researchers argued.
item.dc:creator: Franz Lidz

item.title: The 92-Year-Old Mathematician and the Teenage Apprentice
item.description: Joan Birman thought her major discoveries were behind her. Then came an email from a young neighbor — a girl who knew little but wanted to learn.
item.dc:creator: Gregory Barber
item.media:credit: Oliver Farshi for The New York Times

item.title: Is There Alien Debris on the Moon? Some Scientists Plan to Find Out.
item.description: Researchers want to explore the idea that microscopic particles shed by alien civilizations have accumulated on the lunar surface, making it an archive of extraterrestrial technology.
item.dc:creator: Becky Ferreira
item.media:description: Harrison H. Schmitt, an Apollo 17 astronaut, on his way to take samples on the lunar surface in 1972. Scientists propose sending a lunar mission to sift through about a cubic meter of soil to screen for materials.

item.title: The Heart Drug Pelacarsen Fails, Shocking Novartis and Cardiologists
item.description: Doctors were hopeful the drug, which was being tested in a large clinical trial by Novartis, was going to be a powerful new tool to fight heart disease.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:description: An illustration of lipoprotein(a), a low-density lipoprotein. Every study short of a randomized clinical trial had indicated that the drug would lower Lp(a) and help protect people from heart disease.

item.title: Pentagon Agreement With N.I.H. on Biodefense Draws Alarm From Democrats
item.description: Under a new partnership, the Defense Department would play a larger role in biodefense and pandemic preparedness. Democrats warned it could allow a Pentagon cash grab.
item.dc:creator: Catie Edmondson and Carolyn Y. Johnson
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
item.media:description: The agreement, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, is focused on chemical and biological defense research.

item.title: Hideki Shirakawa, Who Helped Turn a Lab Error Into a Nobel, Dies at 90
item.description: The Japanese chemist played a key role in the discovery of electricity-conducting plastics, largely by accident.
item.dc:creator: Dylan Loeb McClain
item.media:description: Hideki Shirakawa in Stockholm in 2000, when he shared the Nobel Prize. From a young age, he developed an ambition to work in the lab with plastics.

item.title: The World’s First Bugs Had Way More Legs
item.description: Meet the earliest known insects. Shaking hands with them will take a while.
item.dc:creator: Kate Golembiewski
